newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Fla. says tobacco deal weeks off at best.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Fla. says tobacco deal weeks off at best.

text.p: Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth said on Thursday bargaining on an out-of-court settlement of Florida's $1 billion anti-tobacco lawsuit had yet to bear a firm offer from either side.

Butterworth told Reuters that no deal was imminent in Florida's Medicaid case, the next of 40 such suits scheduled to go to trial after Mississippi's settlement announced earlier Thursday, until near the trial date of August 4.
Butterworth denied any settlement was close at hand and said he last met tobacco negotiators on June 26 and did not expect to bargain again for at least another two weeks.

"We're four weeks away from jury selection. It'll be another month before a judge will hear opening statements .... Given the fact our case is at least a couple months away, I think it would be a little premature for both sides to discuss settlement in the Florida case," he said.
Butterworth said last week's meeting lasted just a few hours, with the state and the cigarette companies far apart on many issues.

"We spent a couple of hours across the table last week and came to the conclusion real, real quickly that there was just no way that Florida could settle at this point in time," Butterworth said. "We're just too far off."

Butterworth applauded fellow Attorney General Mike Moore of Mississippi, who reached an agreement late Wednesday putting off next week's start of a trial on Mississippi's lawsuit claiming costs from tobacco companies for treating sick smokers. "I'm very pleased he settled the case and did not delay the case," Butterworth said. "Delaying the case would not have been advantageous to any of the states."
Florida and Mississippi were among the first of 40 states which have sued U.S. cigarette companies for billions of dollars spent on treating sick smokers through Medicaid healthcare programs.

A broad pact settling the suits for $368.5 billion and covering regulation of cigarette marketing was reached on June 20, but the pact faces an uncertain future in Congress. Both Congress and President Clinton must approve that deal.
Moore's agreement with tobacco companies settling Mississippi's suit, the first in the nation, calls for payments of $3 billion but would be superseded by the June 20 pact if it came into force.
